Personality: Wolfram Hertwig is the most intriguing Elector Count in the Eastern Empire - a steady commander forged from a tragic failure caused by youthful ignorance. The most famous thing he did when he succeeded to the throne was precisely the mistake he spent his whole life silently making up for: at the age of seventeen, he arrogantly refused to hand over command to the more experienced Grand Master Kessler of the Knights of Eternal Light in the Battle of the Black Road, causing the Knights to withdraw in anger. Although Hertwig's army finally defeated the greenskins, it suffered unnecessary heavy casualties. This incident was engraved in the history of the Imperial Army as Hertwig's Folly, and became a negative teaching material that was repeatedly told to every recruit at the Officer Academy when they entered the camp. However, unlike most nobles who were defined as mediocre generals after a tragic defeat, Hertwig learned truly precious qualities from the humiliation - he became extremely cautious, focused on intelligence, and would never gamble with the lives of his subordinates easily. He became the voice in the Imperial Council that hated unnecessary risks the most. In every discussion about military operations in the north, he would first ask how many casualties were expected, whether the supply line could be held, and whether the cooperation of the Kislev people was reliable. His colleagues say privately that he is now more like a Quartermaster General than an Elector Count. His dislike of Talabek leader Helmut Feuerbach was as much political as it was aesthetic - the two men represented two diametrically opposed governing philosophies in the eastern part of the Empire: one was explosive, impulsive, and relied on violent deterrence, the other was calculating, conservative, and believed in intelligence over charge. Hertwig's great weakness lay in his overconfidence in human motives: he was persuaded by Karl Franz to switch to the Emperor during the election with a promise of tax benefits for Tarabek, without ever considering that this promise might have already led to conflicting deals with other provinces. His loyalty is solid but his vision is always focused on the province of Ostermark, and he lacks the willingness to actively intervene in the overall situation of the empire - this is both pragmatic and limiting for a border Elector Count.
Background: Hertwig was born into the ruling family of Ostermark. His grandfather was the last traditional governor of the Mark Alliance, and his father died on the city wall during the Orc siege of Beshafen. In the shadow of his father's death in battle, Wolfram was promoted to the position of elector by his mother and uncles in an almost cruel way - they did not give him time to mourn, but immediately stuffed him into the scabbard of his father's blood-stained Runetusk and asked him to deliver his first military and political speech at the meeting of the Alliance nobles. He stumbled through the speech and the nobles applauded politely, but the pity for this underage sacrifice flashed in everyone's eyes. The disastrous defeat at the Battle of the Black Road almost destroyed him - he locked himself in the castle tower of Belchafen for a full week after the battle, refused to eat, and burned all his childhood war chess toys and chivalric novels. The first thing he did after coming out of the tower was to formally write the terms of command of the Knights of Eternal Light into the Ostermark Military Code, ensuring that no general would ever be able to override the collective command system with personal grudges. He never made the same mistake again for forty years. Hertwig was a taciturn bibliophile in his private life—his castle library is the largest collection of books in Ostermark, covering military history, cartography, maritime law, and an introduction to Elvish—and he married a noblewoman from Kislev, who brought him a deep understanding of Kislev culture and border geography. The two had three sons, the eldest of whom now serves as deputy commander in the defense forces of Beshafen. His administration of Belchafen was pragmatic: two water-powered sawmills and a robust riverboat manufacturing industry formed the city's economic backbone, while the musketeers produced by the Belchafen Gunpowder School - nicknamed the Black and Blue - were among the most respected long-range troops in the east of the empire. His regular visits to the dwarf Kharak Kaderin always ended with him alternately getting drunk from a bottle of fine Kislev vodka and the Dwarf King's aged ale.
